extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for when a court should grant, deny, or modify preliminary injunctions in patent cases, including factors justifying bonds/accounts and who may be enjoined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction withheld when it would be useless to plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused where it is useless to the plaintiff on account of the existence of another order of the same character or because no injury will result to him from its denial, or where there has been acquiescence by the public or the issue is doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: refusal where another order already in force; public acquiescence; doubtful legal question. (See cited cases such as Tillinghast v. Hicks.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal of injunction on a re-issue that is broader than the original
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction on a re-issue will be refused where the re-issue is broader than the original until that question is settled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will withhold preliminary relief if validity/scope of the reissue is in doubt; cases cited include Steam Gauge & Lantern Co. v. Miller and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: No injunction on a re-issue to prevent infringement of previously disclaimed inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: No injunction will be granted on a re-issue to prevent the infringement of inventions previously disclaimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the re-issue deliberately disclaims particular subject matter, courts will not enjoin infringement of that disclaimed matter (e.g., Leggett v. Avery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction granted when valid claims of re-issue are infringed
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be granted when the valid claims of a re-issue are infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where some re-issue claims may be invalid, if there exist valid re-issue claims that are infringed, an injunction may issue (see Starrett v. Athol Mach. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may consider plaintiff's standing in trade
rubrics_metrics.description: The standing of the plaintiff in their trade is a matter of importance and may be considered as a reason for an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff's reputation/standing in trade can influence equitable relief (Irwin v. Dane and similar authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether defendant makes and sells or only uses is material
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a material question whether the defendant makes and sells or only uses the plaintiff's invention; the former is treated as an increasing wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are more inclined to enjoin manufacturers/sellers than mere users (e.g., Morris v. Lowell Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: More readily grant injunction against seller than maker
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will issue more easily against a mere seller than against a maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sellers who profit from distribution are more culpable; cases such as Covert v. Curtis illustrate this tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal of injunction against mere user where case is doubtful or inconvenience favors defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction ought to be refused against the mere user (not being the maker or seller) if the case is doubtful or the balance of inconvenience is on the defendant's side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the defendant is only a user and not responsible, equity may withhold an injunction if uncertainty or disproportionate inconvenience exists (see Howe v. Newton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal when injury to defendant substantial relative to plaintiff's benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the injury to the defendant would be out of all proportion to the benefit accruing to the plaintiff, the court may refuse to interrupt the defendant's operations until the necessity for relief is made apparent on final hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include situations where the invention is part of a wider essential process and its stoppage would ruin the defendant's enterprise; courts may require compensation or wait for final hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: No injunction when another suit already has equivalent order
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will not be granted while another injunction to the same effect is already in force in a different suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid duplicative or conflicting preliminary relief (see Gold & Stock Telegraph Co. v. Pearce).

rubrics_metrics.name: No preliminary injunction to compel performance when duty doubtful on final hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction will not be issued to compel an act when on final hearing the duty to perform it may be doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts avoid compelling actions that might be reversed on the merits (e.g., Westinghouse Air Brake Co. v. Carpenter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal where plaintiff and defendant are rival manufacturers and patent covers only part of larger machine
rubrics_metrics.description: No injunction will be granted where the plaintiff and defendant are rival manufacturers and the patent covers only part of a larger machine which cannot be dispensed with except at great loss, a royalty being tendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In competitive manufacturing contexts, courts may prefer licensing/royalty arrangements to injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction may be refused where it does little good to plaintiff but much harm to defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused where it will do the plaintiff little good and the defendant much harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable balancing of harms is applied (Hockholzer v. Eager).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant injunction where plaintiff's right and infringement are clear despite hardship
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will issue where the plaintiff's right is clear and the infringement is established, even though the injunction may cause hardship to the defendant or third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts prioritize protection of patentee's rights if right/infringement are clear (Morris v. Lowell Mfg. Co.; Sickels v. Tileston).

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue injunction when validity, title, and intent to infringe are fully proved and no inequitable circumstances exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the validity of the patent, the title of the plaintiff and the intention of the defendant to infringe are fully proved, and neither other circumstances nor public interest render the grant inequitable, the court will issue an injunction without reluctance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the ordinary rule favoring injunctions once key elements are made out and no equitable bar appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: No injunction where device needed for public use and plaintiff can be otherwise protected
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will not be granted where the device is needed for public use and the plaintiff can be otherwise protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public necessity can outweigh private rights unless absolute right of the plaintiff plainly exists (see Bliss v. City of Brooklyn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction denied where it would occasion great public injury unless absolute right
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be denied where it would occasion great public injury, unless in a case of absolute right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public injury is a strong equitable consideration limiting preliminary relief (Blake v. Greenwood Cemetery example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdict at law establishing right may justify injunction to prevent future violations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a trial at law has resulted in a verdict in favor of the patentee fully establishing the improvement patented, such a trial and result afford sufficient proof to authorize a court to grant an injunction to prevent future violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior final judgment for the patentee often suffices for equitable relief without further proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond and account may be ordered instead of injunction where equity or public interest requires
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar circumstances that lead a court to deny an injunction may induce it to modify the order and require a bond and a continuing account from the defendant rather than enjoining him outright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used where final relief might be denied on same proofs, where validity is doubtful, where plaintiff has been negligent, patent near expiration, or where the defendant would suffer disproportionate injury; examples given throughout text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond ordered when validity in dispute and public acquiescence denied
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond will be ordered instead of an injunction when the validity of the patent is in dispute, has never been adjudged, and public acquiescence is denied and not proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting a bond allows commerce to continue while protecting patentee financially (e.g., Morris v. Shelbourne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond ordered where patentee has been negligent in enforcing rights or patent about to expire
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee has been negligent in asserting his rights, or the patent is about to expire, the court may deny an injunction and order a bond to secure payment of accruing damages and profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable considerations like laches or short remaining term favor money security over injunction (see Jones v. Merrill; Howe v. Morton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond ordered where defendant's device is essential to business or where injunction would cause irreparable injury
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant's device is essential to his business, is made under a later patent, or an injunction would do him irreparable injury, a bond and account may be ordered rather than an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include later-patent good-faith manufacture, potential ruin of enterprise, and inability to extricate invention without unwarrantable injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond amount and account description requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond, when substituted for an injunction, should be sufficient in amount to cover all probable losses to the plaintiff, and the account must so describe the articles sold or used that any person acquainted with the business can fix their value and compute their profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical requirement: bond must cover likely damages; accounts must permit ascertainment of sales and profits for later accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond may be ordered where defendant intends to contest suit and is responsible
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond may be ordered instead of an injunction where the defendant is responsible and intends to contest the suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows defendant to continue business while protecting plaintiff's monetary interests (American Middlings Purifier Co. v. Christian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond substituted where plaintiff grants licenses or has not used the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond may be ordered (and injunction refused) where the patentee grants licenses, does not use the invention, or is guilty of laches or misleading the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing activity, non-use, or equitable estoppel elements support monetary security rather than injunctive restraint (Westinghouse Air Brake Co. v. Carpenter examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond may replace injunction pending higher court review
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond will be ordered rather than an injunction pending a writ of error in the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserves status quo and commerce while appeal is pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any person who may perpetrate, participate in, or derive advantage from infringement may be enjoined
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person, natural or artificial, who in the opinion of the court may be about to perpetrate or participate in an infringing act, or to derive a direct advantage from its performance, may be made defendant and enjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies broadly to direct infringers, conspirators, and beneficiaries; includes municipal and private corporations, stockholders, servants, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal corporations may be enjoined
rubrics_metrics.description: A municipal corporation may be enjoined from practising the invention through its agents, or from permitting infringing contractors to violate the patent for its benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cities can be sued in equity to prevent public contracts from using infringing methods (Bliss v. City of Brooklyn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private corporations, stockholders, and servants may be enjoined when aiding infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Private corporations may be ordered to refrain from authorizing or accepting the results of an infringement; the same prohibition may be extended to their stockholders or servants if they infringe jointly or aid in the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stockholders and officers may be made parties where they actively participate in or profit from the infringement (Poppenhusen v. Falke).

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner may enjoin former partners after dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The owner of a patent may enjoin his former partners after the dissolution of the firm, though during continuance their right to use may have been equal by agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partnership termination restores exclusive rights enforceable in equity (Pentlarge v. Beeston).

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-owner may be enjoined by another co-owner
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may be granted at the instance of one owner of a patent against an infringing co-owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-owners do not have unlimited mutual liberty to infringe each other's rights in a way that harms the other owner (Duke v. Graham).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee with notice is liable to be restrained like assignor
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee taking title with notice of a pending injunction occupies toward the plaintiff the same position as his assignor and is liable at once to be restrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchasers with notice cannot escape injunction simply by assignment; they step into vendor's shoes as to pending equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensees who exceed privileges may be enjoined; innocent overuse ordinarily not enjoined if ceased on notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensees who exceed privileges conferred by their license, or who practise the invention after repudiating their contract, may be enjoined; but where a licensee transcends rights through accident or mistake and upon notice ceases to infringe, the court will ordinarily refuse to issue an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent and willful excess matter: deliberate overuse invites injunction, inadvertent excess that is corrected often will not.

rubrics_metrics.name: A licensee under one co-owner will not be enjoined at suit of the other co-owner
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee under one co-owner of the patent will not be enjoined at the suit of the other co-owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licenses granted by one co-owner protect licensee against suits by that co-owner, but disputes among co-owners involve different rules (Clum v. Brewer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partners of licensees enjoy immunity while firm fulfills obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The partner of a licensee enjoys the immunity bestowed on his copartner by the license and is not subject to injunction while the firm fulfills its obligations to the licensor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firm-level licenses extend protection to partners acting within the license's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agents and salesmen may be enjoined and treated as principals if evidence supports it
rubrics_metrics.description: Though a defendant may claim to be an agent, he will be treated as a principal if the infringing article bears his name and other evidence points to him as primarily responsible; actual agents who sell infringing articles on behalf of their maker or owner are also liable to an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to substance over form; agents with active roles in sales/distribution can be enjoined even without ownership interest (Maltby v. Bobo; Steiger v. Heidelberger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppliers of tools/materials — liability to injunction doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether those who contribute to the infringing act by furnishing tools and materials therefor, in the due course of business and without participation in the act or its direct results, can be enjoined is doubted; their connection appears too remote to warrant the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are reluctant to enjoin ordinary suppliers who merely provide components absent active participation or intent to promote infringement.
